questions.q: You write const limit = 10; and later limit = 20;. What happens when the code runs?
questions.explain: A const binding can never point at a new value. Assigning to it throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable. Use let when the value must change.
options: It throws a TypeError: assignment to a constant variable
limit stays 10 and nothing is printed
It works only inside a function

questions.q: Which should you use by default for a new variable?
questions.explain: Start with const: it tells the reader (and you) that the value never changes. Use let for counters and values you update. Avoid var, whose scope rules cause bugs.
options: const, and switch to let only when the value must change
let, because it is shorter to change later

questions.q: Why does the lesson tell you to avoid var?
questions.explain: var belongs to the whole function, not the block { … } it is written in. That makes values leak out of loops and if blocks. let and const stay inside their block.
options: It ignores block scope, so a variable declared inside an if or a loop leaks out of it

questions.q: Which of these is a valid variable name?
questions.explain: Names cannot start with a digit, cannot contain - (that is the minus operator), and cannot be a reserved word like let. JavaScript code uses camelCase: taskCount.

questions.q: A const variable holds an object. What does this print?
questions.explain: const stops the variable from pointing at another value. The object itself can still change, so setting task.done works.

questions.explain: Quotes make a string, so "42" is a string even though it looks like a number. typeof undefined is the string "undefined".

questions.q: What does typeof null give?
questions.explain: This is a famous mistake from the first version of JavaScript that can never be fixed. To check for null, compare directly: value === null.

questions.q: Which of these is not a primitive type in JavaScript?
questions.explain: The seven primitives are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Arrays are objects: typeof [1, 2] is "object".

questions.q: A form sends the quantity as text. What does this print?
questions.explain: + with a string joins text, so "2" + 1 is "21". * only works on numbers, so JavaScript converts "2" to 2 and gets 6. This silent conversion is called coercion.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Number() converts on purpose. An empty string becomes 0 (a common surprise), text that is not a number becomes NaN, and true becomes 1. Always check for empty input before converting.

questions.q: Which is the clearest way to turn the number price into a string on purpose?
questions.explain: String(price) says exactly what you mean. price + "" also works, but relies on coercion, which is easy to misread.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Backticks make a template literal. Anything inside ${ } is evaluated, so open * 2 becomes 6.

questions.explain: Numbers are stored in binary, and 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be stored exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. toFixed(2) rounds it for display and returns a string.

questions.q: You store prices for a shop. How should you avoid rounding errors like 0.1 + 0.2?
questions.explain: Whole numbers (up to about 9 quadrillion) are exact. Keep money in the smallest unit and convert only when you show it. Adding strings with + would join them.
options: Store whole cents as integers (e.g. 1999 for 19.99) and divide only for display
Round every number with Math.round before storing
Store prices as strings like "19.99" and add them with +

questions.explain: parseInt and parseFloat read digits from the start and stop at the first character they do not understand. If the text does not start with a number, they return NaN.

questions.q: How do you check whether value is NaN?
questions.explain: NaN is the only value not equal to itself, so value === NaN is always false. Use Number.isNaN(value). typeof NaN is "number".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: round goes to the nearest whole number (halves go up), floor always down, ceil always up, and max returns the largest argument.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JavaScript does not throw on division by zero. It returns Infinity, -Infinity or NaN, so check your divisor yourself.

questions.q: Which of these values is truthy?
questions.explain: The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including the string "0" and an empty array.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An empty array is an object, and every object is truthy. The string "false" is not empty, so it is truthy too. 0n is the bigint zero, which is falsy.

questions.q: What is the usual difference between undefined and null?
questions.explain: JavaScript gives you undefined for a variable without a value, a missing property or a missing argument. You write null yourself, for example dueDate: null for "no due date".
options: undefined means "no value was ever given"; null is a value you set on purpose to mean "nothing"
They are exactly the same value with two names
null is for numbers and undefined for strings

questions.q: Prices are stored in cents. Finish formatPrice so formatPrice(1999) returns "$19.99" and formatPrice(5) returns "$0.05".
questions.explain: Divide by 100 only for display, and use toFixed(2) to always show two decimals.

questions.q: A form sends quantities as text. Finish parseQuantity: return the number when the text is a whole number from 1 to 99, otherwise return null. Watch out for empty text, which Number("") turns into 0.
questions.explain: Reject empty text first, then use Number.isInteger, which is false for NaN and for 2.5, and finally check the range.
